title: Who Shares Fake News Intentionally and Unintentionally on Social Media? The Case of Facebook Users in Poland
screen_reason: Two-wave online survey of 1,000 active Facebook news users in Poland (December 2019 - January 2020) asking whether the respondent has ever shared a political news story they thought at the time was made up (intentional) or later found out was made up (unintentional). Those are self-reported sharing shares, so RECALL/sharing. The catch, flagged on both rows: the paper reports these percentages ONLY by latent SML class (Table 5), never as an overall share of the sample, and R8 forbids computing the class-weighted total.

estimates.platform: Facebook (sample of active Facebook news users; item wording says 'online')
estimates.date: December 2019 to January 2020 (two waves 7-10 days apart)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who report ever having shared a political news story online that they thought at the time was made up (intentional sharing)
estimates.value_raw: By latent SML class only (Table 5, class Ns from Table 4): class 1 16.67% (N=96), class 2 26.15% (N=65), class 3 7.94% (N=126), class 4 16.98% (N=265), class 5 21.15% (N=383), class 6 29.23% (N=65). No overall percentage reported.
estimates.denominator: 1,000 active Facebook users in Poland recruited from the largest Polish research panel, all of whom use Facebook at least a few times a week and consume news there (932 after dropping 68 'no answer' responses for the regression models)
estimates.definition: Answered 'yes' to: 'Have you ever shared a political news story online that you thought at the time was made up?'
estimates.misinfo_def: "For the purpose of this study, fake news is understood as partially or completely false information, intended to mislead the recipient, which may be intentionally and unintentionally disseminated by online news consumers"
estimates.page_loc: p. 175 (Variables) and p. 180 (Table 5, 'Sharing of fake news', column 'Intentional')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent's own recall and own judgement of the story's falsity; no content collected or verified. Single binary item (yes/no/no answer), lifetime window ('ever').
estimates.moderator_quote: Our study used a convenience sample as there is no sampling frame of Facebook users in Poland. Only those (i) actively using Facebook (at least a few times a week) and (ii) consuming news from sources available on this platform were invited to take part.
estimates.notes: ADJUDICATION FLAG - no poolable point estimate. The overall share of respondents answering yes is never reported; the values exist only for six latent classes derived from a social media literacy scale (analytic, not demographic, subgroups). value_kind=range_not_point with the six class values in value_raw rather than 6 separate subgroup rows. The class-weighted mean would be about 19%, but R8 forbids a cross-category computation, so no value_pct is given. Also note the paper's text miscomputes: 'the most engaged (80%)' for class 6 and 'almost 20%' for class 3 are the SUM of the intentional and unintentional percentages, which are not mutually exclusive categories, so those two figures are not usable. Item wording is 'online', not 'on Facebook', although the sample is Facebook news users and the paper frames results as Facebook sharing throughout.

estimates.notes: Same structural problem as the intentional row: values exist only per latent SML class, never pooled; class-weighted mean would be about 28% but R8 forbids computing it. definition_variant=true because this is the same self-reported sharing measure under a different awareness condition (found out afterwards rather than suspected at the time) in the same country x platform cell. Unintentional exceeds intentional in every class.

missed_or_uncertain: 1) The single most important gap: no overall prevalence. The paper never states what share of the 1,000 respondents answered yes to either sharing item; only Table 5's six latent-class percentages exist. All twelve values are listed verbatim in the two rows' value_raw so nothing is lost. If the review's rules allowed a class-weighted computation, the totals would be roughly 19% intentional and 28% unintentional (Ns 96/65/126/265/383/65 summing to 1,000), but R8 forbids it and these are NOT reported by the authors. 2) The paper's own summary figures '80%' (class 6) and 'almost 20%' (class 3) are arithmetic sums of the intentional and unintentional percentages, which are not mutually exclusive response categories; they overstate the number of sharers and should not be used. 3) Not extracted, ineligible: all regression coefficients (Table 3), the SML scale psychometrics (Cronbach alpha > 0.88, EFA four factors explaining 51% of variance), and the latent class profile means in Table 4 and the Appendix (age, salary, trust in Facebook, SML score). 4) No exposure or content measure exists in this paper: nobody was asked how much fake news they saw, and no content was collected, so there is no CONTENT, EXPOSURE, REACH or CONCENTRATION row available. 5) Sample composition figures (48.5% male, 49% with a master's degree) are demographics, not misinformation.

rob.design: Two-wave CAWI survey (waves 7-10 days apart) fielded December 2019 - January 2020 by a third party from the largest research panel in Poland; 1,000 respondents, all screened for using Facebook at least a few times a week AND consuming news on Facebook. Explicitly a convenience sample: 'there is no sampling frame of Facebook users in Poland', though the authors report the sample matches Polish Facebook users and the general population on gender, residence and education (Table 1, benchmarked against Megapanel PBI/Gemius 2015 and Statistical Yearbook of Poland 2020). No response rate or panel cooperation rate reported. Both outcome measures are single binary self-report items with a lifetime window and no external verification; 68 'no answer' cases dropped, leaving N = 932 for the models. Social media literacy measured with the Koc and Barut New Media Literacy Scale (12 items, Cronbach alpha > 0.88; EFA four factors explaining 51% of variance; three functional-prosumption items dropped for cross-loading). Analysis by backward-stepwise GLM and a six-class latent class analysis (BIC 20359). Authors list non-representativeness, single country and single platform as limitations.
rob.item6_quote: For the purpose of this study, fake news is understood as partially or completely false information, intended to mislead the recipient, which may be intentionally and unintentionally disseminated by online news consumers (Baptista and Gradim 2020; Lazer et al. 2018).
rob.item10_quote: Our dependent variables were made of the following research item: (i) DV1 Have you ever shared a political news story online that you thought at the time was made up? (intentional sharing), (ii) DV2 Have you ever shared a political news story online that you later found out was made up? (unintentional sharing). Responses to both questions were measured on the nominal scale containing three options: (a) yes, (b) no, (c) no answer.
